facts.claim: InstructGPT (Ouyang and colleagues, 2022) was made in three stages: fine-tuning GPT-3 on answers people wrote, collecting people’s rankings of the model’s outputs, then reinforcement learning from that human feedback.
In the InstructGPT paper, people preferred the answers of the 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT to those of the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3, a model about 100 times bigger.
Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov and colleagues, 2023) trains on preference pairs with a simple classification loss, with no separate reward model and no reinforcement learning loop.
The DPO paper shows the policy it aims for: the reference model’s odds, scaled up by the reward, with a parameter β controlling how far it may stray from the reference.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (DeepSeekMath, 2024) drops PPO’s critic model: it samples a group of answers per question and scores each against the group’s average reward, divided by the group’s spread.
Tülu 3 (2024) named Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards: the model gets a reward only when its answer is verified correct, on tasks such as maths and checkable instructions.
DeepSeek-R1-Zero (2025) was trained by large-scale reinforcement learning with no supervised fine-tuning first; it reasoned well but its answers were hard to read and mixed languages.
Gao and colleagues (2022) found that a reward model is an imperfect stand-in for what people want, so optimising its score too far can make real quality worse: Goodhart’s law.
DeepMind (2020) calls it specification gaming when an agent meets the literal objective without the intended outcome, like a boat that circles hitting reward targets instead of finishing its race.
